item.text: {"text":"Recent research separates broad similarity from practical fit. [ECCR (2024)](https://genai-personalization.github.io/assets/papers/GenAIRecP2024/Li.pdf) shows why co-purchase and category relevance cannot establish complementarity: an accessory must also fit the specific anchor item. [Intent diversification (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3690624.3709429) distinguishes diversity of user purposes from item dissimilarity. For this task, these findings suggest auditable probes: TF-IDF overlap with recent versus older history; overlap in distinctive title phrases or model identifiers; near-duplicate title/description rates within recommendations; and explicit compatibility statements or conflicting identifiers. Treat these as lexical evidence, with source snippets, rather than confirmed intent, redundancy, substitution or compatibility. Interaction proximity alone cannot resolve those relationships.\n\nUncertainty should accompany each diagnostic. [ExUA (2024)](https://www.amazon.science/publications/explainable-uncertainty-attribution-for-sequential-recommendation) attributes sequential recommendation uncertainty to historical interactions using gradient saliency. A simpler proposed audit can measure score/rank changes after removing recent history events, without fitting additional predictors; sensitivity is not calibrated confidence. Report title/description availability, compatibility-evidence coverage, unknown cases and metric denominators separately by category. For the twenty training users, compare suspected duplicates or incompatibilities against explicit rejection reasons, distinguishing “already have/same purpose,” “wrong model/format,” and “irrelevant now”; retain ambiguous responses as unknown. Report agreement counts and user-level uncertainty, recognizing only five users per category. These are proposed task adaptations, not validated findings from this benchmark; absent feedback cannot establish rejection, and neither histories nor metadata establish unobserved simulator traits."}
